summary: Pupils aged 12–13 build and wield the three-fates model: at any boundary a wave is reflected, absorbed, or transmitted (usually a split of all three), with absorbed energy conserved as heat. The load-bearing idea is that the outcome depends on the MATERIAL and the WAVE'S FREQUENCY TOGETHER, not either alone. Learners test a material×band grid, then transfer the model to three contexts — colour as selective reflection, sight, and band-matched communication technologies — and confront the X-ray puzzle that breaks the intuitive 'big waves slip through' story.
misconceptions: 'Big waves slip through, small waves are blocked' (size-only) — a useful stepping stone but incomplete and misleading; it cannot explain glass vs brick vs metal, and the X‑ray puzzle (short wavelength, yet transmitted through flesh) breaks it outright. The real determinant is how the material's electrons respond to that frequency.

'Transmission only happens through transparent things / if I can't see through it, nothing gets through' — but a brick wall is opaque to light yet transparent to radio. Transparency is wavelength-specific, not a blanket property.

Treating reflect/absorb/transmit as a FIXED, single property of a material ('mirrors reflect, black things absorb, glass transmits') rather than depending on the wave's frequency too — the same glass transmits visible, absorbs UV, and transmits radio.
'Absorbed light just disappears / is destroyed' — absorbed energy is conserved and becomes heat (thermal/infra-red); this is the greenhouse and dark-clothes effect.

Colour is an innate property of an object regardless of lighting (carried from the colour topic) — colour is the set of frequencies REFLECTED/transmitted, so it depends on the illuminating light; a red object under blue light looks black.

Not seeing WHY different comms bands are chosen — pupils think the choice is arbitrary rather than driven by which fate the band undergoes in air/walls/fibre (radio penetrates and travels far; visible light is trapped by walls but guided perfectly down a fibre).
'Radio always passes, light never does' as an absolute — penetration depends on material and thickness (metal blocks radio; metres of rock attenuate it), and glass lets light straight through.

activities.title: Materials & waves bench: sweep one variable, watch the fate change
steps: Pick a material slab (glass, brick, metal, water, skin, black card) and a frequency band (radio, microwave, infrared, visible, UV, X-ray), then fire the wave and observe it split into a reflected ray, an absorbed share (the slab visibly warms / an infrared readout climbs), and a transmitted ray.
Read the energy bar showing the three shares always summing to the incoming energy (100%), confirming nothing is lost.

Keep the SAME ordinary window-glass slab fixed and sweep the band: watch visible light pass mostly straight through, most ultraviolet (especially UVB) get absorbed (window glass greatly reduces sunburn, though some UVA still gets through), and radio pass again — recording what the one material does to each wave.
Fill in a material×band grid by predicting each cell's dominant fate (mostly reflect / absorb / transmit) BEFORE testing it, then correcting predictions against what the bench shows.
Switch to a communications mode: send a signal from a basement to the street and watch radio get through while a visible beam is trapped; then watch a fibre guide visible light around a corner.
Switch to a colour mode: send white light at a coloured slab, see absorbed frequencies greyed out and the reflected frequency reach the eye, and connect this to the visible-light cell of the grid.
activities.insight: Whether a wave is reflected, absorbed, or transmitted depends on both the material and the wave's frequency acting together; absorbed energy becomes heat; and reflect/absorb/transmit is NOT a fixed single property of a material.

activities.title: Break the size-only story with the X-ray puzzle
steps: Lay radio (long wavelength), visible (mid), and X-ray (short wavelength) on a wavelength axis against ONE stated material — flesh — and note, for that material, which pass and which are blocked: through flesh, radio passes, visible is blocked, and X-ray passes.
State the intuitive 'bigger waves slip through, smaller waves get blocked' rule and test it against these three cases for the one material.
Explain why the rule fails: X-rays have a very short wavelength yet pass through flesh (while mid-wavelength visible is blocked), so wavelength/size alone cannot be the determinant.

As a KS4-stretch direction of travel, reframe the real cause qualitatively: it points toward how the material's electrons respond to that particular frequency, rather than the wave's size — not a computed account at this age.
activities.insight: A size-only argument is only a stepping stone; it cannot explain glass vs brick vs metal and is broken outright by X-rays passing through flesh, so the determinant is really material-and-frequency together (pointing, as a KS4 stretch, toward how a material responds to a given frequency).

activities.title: Fold colour and communications back into the one model
steps: Explain why a red jumper looks red in daylight using absorb/reflect/transmit — stating what happens to the other colours that land on it.

Explain the opposite extreme: a black surface looks black because it absorbs (almost) all the visible frequencies that land on it and reflects very little, while a white surface reflects nearly all of them.
Predict what a red object looks like under blue light and justify it (it would reflect red, but there is no red light present to reflect, so it appears dark/black).

Match each band to a technology with the REASON: radio for through-walls/long-range broadcast, the microwave atmospheric 'window' for satellite links, infrared for short-range line-of-sight (remotes) and fibre, visible light for fibre optics.
Explain the microwave-oven door mesh: it lets visible light out (you see your food) while reflecting the microwaves back in — the same object doing different things to different waves.

Explain why you feel warm in sunlight through a closed cool window: transmitted visible and near-infrared sunlight is absorbed by surfaces (and your skin) inside, warming them, while the glass transmits most of it and so stays relatively cool.
activities.insight: Colour, sight, and communications are all instances of the same three-fates model: colour is the frequencies an object reflects/transmits rather than absorbs (black absorbs almost all visible light, white reflects almost all), and comms bands are chosen because of which fate they undergo in air, walls, or fibre.

activities.title: Predict-observe-explain: foil versus wool around a radio
steps: Play a small FM radio or a phone streaming a clear station.
Before wrapping it fully in aluminium foil, predict with a reason whether the signal survives; then wrap and test.
Before wrapping it (fresh) in a thick wool sock, predict with a reason whether the signal survives; then wrap and test.

Compare the two results — a complete, gap-free foil wrap typically weakens the signal greatly or cuts it out, while wool barely affects it — and explain each: the metal foil mainly reflects radio (a Faraday-cage effect) so little gets through, while wool transmits most of it; if some signal survives the foil, check for gaps or a very strong station.

Articulate the rule the demo supports: thickness alone does not decide the fate (thin foil blocked more than thick wool), so the fate depends on material × wave; note that foil is also denser than wool, so this demo alone cannot rule out density — use the fixed-glass sweep (same material, different waves) to show density is not the whole story.
activities.insight: Blocking is not simply about thickness; thin metal foil reflects radio while thick wool transmits it, so the outcome depends on how the specific material interacts with that specific wave (density is not a reliable guide either, but this demo cannot show that on its own because foil is denser than wool).

activities.title: Diagnostic explanation: dark brick room, working phone signal
steps: Consider a brick house with the curtains drawn so no light enters and the room is dark, yet a phone still receives a radio signal through the walls.
Explain in writing how radio waves get through the wall when light cannot, stating what the wall does to each wave.

Name the fate of each wave at the wall: visible light absorbed/reflected (so the room is dark), radio largely transmitted through the brick (some is absorbed or reflected, so the signal is weaker indoors).

Generalise: whether a material absorbs, reflects, or transmits a wave depends on both the material and the wave's frequency — a material is not simply a 'blocker' or a 'letter-through' for everything.
Transfer the same reasoning to the oven mesh, a coloured object, and the foil-versus-wool prediction.
activities.insight: The same wall is opaque to light but transparent to radio; explaining this requires treating wave-material interaction as frequency-dependent rather than a single fixed 'blocks everything' behaviour.

checkQuestion: You are sitting in a brick house with the curtains drawn, so NO light gets in from outside — the room is dark. Yet your phone still gets a radio signal through the walls. How can radio waves get through the wall when light can't? Explain what the wall is doing to each.
checkAnswer: The SAME wall interacts differently with different waves. It absorbs and reflects visible light (so the room is dark — the wall is opaque to light), but it TRANSMITS radio waves, whose much longer wavelength passes through the brick. So whether a material absorbs, reflects or transmits a wave depends on BOTH the material and the wave's wavelength — a material isn't simply a 'blocker' or a 'letter-through' for everything.
